Consult Summary:
- Left-sided unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with ipsilateral facial numbness around the left jaw/ear, tinnitus, and intermittent dizziness for ~3 weeks. Working differential includes vestibular schwannoma, Bell’s palsy, and labyrinthitis; patient will be evaluated in person with neuro/ENT exam to confirm or refine diagnosis.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Left ear hearing loss for ~3 weeks; associated numbness of the left face (around the ear/jawline); occasional tinnitus; intermittent dizziness.
  - No weakness, dysphagia, or vision changes reported.
  - No ear discharge or ear pain; no fever.
  - Numbness persists at present.
- Associated symptoms:
  - Tinnitus; dizziness at times.
- Negatives:
  - No facial weakness documented; no other cranial nerve symptoms noted; no systemic symptoms described.
- Past medical history, allergies, medications:
  - Nasal polyps (historical); prior labyrinthitis (not ongoing).
  - Regular meds: nasal steroid spray PRN; Rennies PRN.
  - Allergies: Latex.
- Social history:
  - Occupation: jockey; training reduced due to symptoms; currently working with reduced activity.
  - Lives with partner; no pets.
- Family history:
  - Brother with Neurofibromatosis (NF) possible, per patient report.
- Other notes:
  - Concern about seriousness expressed by patient; patient desires reassurance and in-person assessment.

Examination:
- Findings documented in transcript:
  - No vital signs provided.
  - No physical exam results recorded yet.
  - Clinician planned in-clinic neurological examination and ENT/ear assessment (to be performed in person) and to look inside the ear.
- Observations from transcript:
  - Symptoms localized to left side (hearing loss and facial numbness); no reported cranial nerve weakness or other focal deficits in the chat.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Primary working consideration includes Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial nerve palsy) as one possible cause of unilateral facial numbness, with concurrent unilateral hearing symptoms suggesting an inner ear or CPA process.
  - Differential includes acoustic vestibular schwannoma (vestibular schwannoma) and labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis, given unilateral SNHL with tinnitus and dizziness, and prior labyrinthitis history.
  - DDx ranking (from system): Acoustic schwannoma often favored for unilateral SNHL with tinnitus/dizziness; Bell’s palsy considered; labyrinthitis possible but less consistent with chronicity and accompanying hearing loss.
- Conflicts noted:
  - Conflict noted between transcript’s emphasis on Bell’s palsy as a probable cause and the DDx ranking which prioritizes acoustic schwannoma as top diagnosis. Transcript-based priority favors immediate in-person neuro exam to clarify; imaging may be considered if exam supports a CPA lesion.

Plan:
- Immediate actions:
  - Schedule in-person face-to-face Neuro/ENT evaluation today in a Central London clinic to perform a comprehensive neurological exam and ear examination.
  - ENT/ear assessment to look for ear pathology, facial nerve involvement, and other cranial nerve signs.
- Follow-up investigations and referrals (as indicated by exam):
  - If examination raises suspicion for vestibular schwannoma or CPA lesion, obtain MRI brain with contrast.
  - Audiology assessment as part of evaluation for unilateral hearing loss.
- Additional recommendations consistent with DDx and transcript:
  - Ensure patient has no red flags requiring urgent care (e.g., progressive new weakness, ataxia, dysphagia) — not reported.
  - Reassurance provided pending exam, with emphasis on not life-threatening at present.
  - Admin support: clinic appointment will be arranged by admin; patient advised to contact support to secure a same-day slot.

Document Quality:
- Missing elements:
  - No vitals documented (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, etc.).
  - No formal neurologic or cranial nerve exam results provided yet.
  - No imaging or labs performed to date.
  - Comprehensive medication list and adherence data not fully detailed beyond PRN meds.
- Conflicts:
  - Explicit conflict noted: DDx prioritizes acoustic schwannoma as top diagnosis, whereas the patient-contacted clinician leaned toward Bell’s palsy as a leading consideration.
- Transcript quality:
  - Medical history and symptoms are described, but exam data are absent; the session lacked objective findings at the time of the call. Clear plan was provided for in-person assessment to obtain definitive findings. Some details (e.g., exact neuro exam results) are missing and will rely on the clinic visit.
